n: The tribal quarrel at the end of chapter 19 explodes. Sheba, a troublemaker from Saul’s tribe of Benjamin, sounds the trumpet and calls the northern tribes to abandon David.

f.g: A worthless, wicked man.

f.w: We have no part in David
f.g: Almost the same cry will split the kingdom after Solomon’s death.
A call to go home — to withdraw support from the king.

n: The northern tribes follow Sheba, but Judah stays loyal and escorts David from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

f.g: Clave = clung to, stayed loyal to.

n: Back in Jerusalem, David places the ten concubines Absalom had violated under guard, providing for them but no longer living with them as wives. They spend their lives like widows — further victims of the family’s tragedy.

f.g: Kept them in a guarded house.

n: David orders his new commander Amasa to gather Judah’s troops within three days.
Amasa takes longer than the time set — perhaps because Judah’s men were slow to follow Absalom’s former general.
Fearing Sheba will grow more dangerous than Absalom, David sends Abishai with the royal troops to chase him before he reaches fortified cities.

f.g: Walled, fortified cities.

n: Joab’s men, the royal guard, and the elite warriors set out from Jerusalem. Joab joins them, though he is no longer officially in command.
At Gibeon, Amasa meets them. Joab arranges his sword so that it falls out of its sheath — likely a deliberate trick to have it in his hand without suspicion.

f.w: the great stone which is in Gibeon
f.g: A landmark rock at Gibeon, near where Joab fought Abner (2 Samuel 2:12-17).

n: Joab greets Amasa warmly, calling him “my brother” and taking his beard as if to kiss him — a customary greeting.

f.w: Art thou in health, my brother?
f.g: Literally “Is it shalom with you?”

n: Amasa doesn’t notice the sword in Joab’s other hand, and Joab kills him with one stroke — exactly as he had killed Abner. Then Joab simply resumes command and pursues Sheba.

f.g: He needed only one blow.

n: One of Joab’s men calls everyone to follow Joab if they support David — linking loyalty to the king with loyalty to Joab.
Amasa’s body lies in the road, stopping the troops in their tracks. The soldier drags it into a field and covers it with a cloth.

f.g: Lay in his own blood.

n: With the body out of sight, the army moves on after Joab.
Sheba travels through the northern tribes to Abel Beth-maachah in the far north, gathering his own clan along the way.

f.g: Abel Beth-maachah, a fortified town near Dan in northern Israel.
Possibly the Bichrites — Sheba’s own clan.

n: Joab besieges the city, building a siege ramp and battering the wall.

f.g: Built an earthen siege ramp up to the wall.

n: A wise woman calls from the wall, asking to speak with Joab.
She confirms she is speaking to Joab and asks him to listen.

f.g: Servant woman — a polite way of referring to herself.

n: She reminds him that Abel was famous for wisdom: people used to say, “Ask advice at Abel,” and disputes were settled there.

f.g: Were wont = used to; it was customary to say.

n: She speaks for her peaceful, loyal city. Why destroy a “mother in Israel” — a major town — and part of the Lord’s inheritance?

f.g: A leading city with dependent villages around it.
God’s land and people.

n: Joab insists he has no desire to destroy the city.

f.g: God forbid; certainly not.

n: He only wants Sheba, the rebel. Hand him over and the army will leave. The woman promises Sheba’s head will be thrown over the wall.

f.g: The hill country of Ephraim, which included parts of Benjamin.

n: Through her wisdom, the townspeople execute Sheba and give his head to Joab. One woman’s counsel saves a whole city. Joab sounds the trumpet and returns to Jerusalem.
Joab is again commander of the army — having regained his post by murder. A list of David’s officials follows.
Adoram oversees forced labor — a new office that shows the kingdom’s growing demands on its people.

f.g: Tribute here = forced labor; also called Adoniram.

n: Sheva serves as secretary, and Zadok and Abiathar as the priests.

f.g: Probably the same official as Seraiah in 2 Samuel 8:17.

n: Ira the Jairite serves as a priest or chief official for David.

f.g: Hebrew kohen, normally “priest”; perhaps a personal priest or royal adviser.
